before: Low-timestep conversion of graph neural networks is often assessed through activation or message reconstruction. What must such reconstruction preserve to retain a graph classifier's decision? We study this question by intervening on hard events in converted superpixel graph classifiers. Two gaps emerge. First, reducing the error of the actual graph message can worsen its downstream class margin: this occurs in 40.9\% and 31.9\% of message-improving interventions on MNIST and CIFAR10, respectively. Second, temporal codes with exactly the same local decoded output and event count can produce different downstream predictions and activity. A directional margin analysis and a source-recurrence counterexample explain why neither message magnitude nor terminal reconstruction determines decision fidelity. Three-teacher position interventions locate a major low-timestep bottleneck at the first node activation, while matched calibration controls distinguish this sensitivity from a realizable correction. Residual centering provides a constructive example of reducing a projection-activity proxy without resolving the decision problem. Together, these results identify the spatial direction and temporal history discarded by reconstruction metrics, and establish practical conditions for evaluating finite-event graph conversion.
after: Activation and message reconstruction are common measures of low-timestep graph conversion, but they summarize only part of the information needed to preserve a classifier's decision. We examine the missing information through hard-event interventions in converted superpixel graph classifiers. Reducing the error of the actual graph message can worsen the downstream teacher-class margin: this occurs in 40.9\% and 31.9\% of message-improving interventions on MNIST and CIFAR10, respectively. Temporal codes with exactly the same local decoded output and event count can also produce different downstream predictions and activity. Directional margin analysis explains the first distinction, while a source-recurrence counterexample isolates the second. Three-teacher position interventions identify the first node activation as a major short-prefix bottleneck; matched calibration controls distinguish this sensitivity from a realizable correction. Residual centering further shows how a representation change can reduce a projection-activity proxy while leaving decision preservation to be evaluated separately. These findings characterize the spatial direction and temporal history lost by reconstruction metrics and motivate evaluating finite-event graph conversion through downstream decisions, required prefixes, and whole-network activity.

before: Graph neural networks make predictions by repeatedly mixing information over a graph. Converting their continuous representations to a small number of events changes both the values being propagated and the histories through which later layers receive them. For visual graphs, this coupling matters: an image-level decision can change when a perturbation at one superpixel crosses a downstream quantization boundary, even if an average reconstruction metric improves.

before: The distinction is sharper than an imperfect correlation between MSE and accuracy. A lower next-message error respects the actual adjacency and weights, but still discards the direction of that error relative to class boundaries. An exact local terminal reconstruction preserves even more information, yet discards intermediate states encountered by downstream event units. These are separate obstacles. A correction may improve the message norm while moving the final decision in the wrong direction; an alternative code may match its local output exactly while changing the downstream computation.
after: Two forms of information loss are relevant. Next-message error uses the actual adjacency and weights, yet its norm discards the perturbation's direction relative to class boundaries. Exact local terminal reconstruction preserves the decoded value, but omits the intermediate states encountered by downstream event units. A correction can therefore reduce message error while moving the final decision toward a competing class; a code can match its local endpoint while changing the downstream trajectory.

before: Our experiments identify two ways in which reconstruction metrics discard information needed for low-timestep graph decisions. A message norm discards direction relative to every competing class, and a terminal reconstruction discards the temporal states through which downstream units evolved. Position recovery shows where an intervention can matter; hard changes establish that a favorable local metric need not improve the decision; exact codeword exchanges reveal the remaining temporal ambiguity even after local terminal error is eliminated.
after: The experiments expose two distinct information losses in reconstruction-based evaluation. Message norms omit the signed direction of an error relative to competing classes, while terminal reconstruction omits the temporal states traversed by downstream units. Position recovery locates influential sites; hard-event changes show that improving a local metric can worsen the decision; exact codeword exchanges demonstrate that eliminating local terminal error still leaves downstream temporal ambiguity.
